title: Multipass pairing heaps: logarithmic amortized delete-min — resolved
formal: Does the standard multipass pairing heap satisfy the following bound? For every valid operation sequence starting with no heaps, let D be the number of delete-min operations, Q the number of all other operations, and N the maximum size of any heap during the sequence. The total number of key comparisons and constant-time pointer operations is at most C[Q + D log₂(N+2)] for a universal C. Allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld and delete-min. The answer is yes, as a consequence of Sinnamon and Tarjan’s theorem.
definitions: Keys are opaque elements of a total order, with distinct keys for simplicity. A nonempty heap is one rooted ordered tree with each parent key smaller than its children’s keys; its root is the minimum. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger-key root the leftmost child of the smaller-key root. Insertion links a singleton with the existing root, or creates the root if empty. Melding consumes two disjoint heaps and links their roots, with empty heaps handled directly. find-min returns the root key. delete-min removes the root and treats its children, in their current left-to-right order, as roots. A pass links the first and second roots, the third and fourth, and so on; an unpaired final root carries over unchanged. The surviving roots remain in their relative order. Repeat complete passes from left to right until at most one root remains. Sibling lists and child pointers support each link in O(1) pointer operations. Valid delete-min and find-min calls use nonempty heaps. N=0 is allowed for sequences containing no inserted item. The bound is over the whole sequence, including a sequence ending with nonempty heaps. Decrease-key is excluded from this precise basic bound; its separate cost is discussed below.
answer_criterion: The historical target is the stated universal sequence bound for this exact pairing schedule. It has been proved. A single delete-min need not take O(log N) actual time; the logarithmic guarantee is amortized across the operation sequence.
context:
Self-adjusting heaps rearrange their trees in response to operations without storing balance ranks or subtree sizes. The multipass rule is especially simple: remove the minimum, pair adjacent roots repeatedly, and retain the smaller root in each pair. The absence of explicit balancing makes the implementation short, but conceals how much future work a link creates.

An individual minimum can have many children. Removing that root therefore may require a linear number of links, even though each pairing pass approximately halves the root list. Counting the number of passes alone does not prove a logarithmic operation cost. The analysis must account for links over an entire sequence.

The 2018 paper reduced the extra factor above logarithmic amortized cost to a very slowly growing expression involving the iterated logarithm. That was a meaningful improvement in the analysis, but it still did not give the exact logarithmic target. The same paper also studies path-balanced search trees; those are a separate algorithm and question.

Sinnamon and Tarjan subsequently obtained logarithmic amortized delete-min, constant-time insertion and melding, and stronger bounds that discount items never deleted. Their theorem also allows decrease-key operations, charging them separately. The displayed formulation keeps only the basic operations so that the claim about delete-min cannot accidentally promise free decrease-key.

This remains in the catalogue as a resolved historical card. It documents how a long-standing analysis problem was settled without changing the familiar multipass algorithm. Keeping the exact pairing order also prevents confusion with the standard two-pass pairing heap, whose second pass accumulates links differently.
why: The problem was a basic test of whether a simple restructuring rule gives optimal amortized priority-queue performance without balance metadata. Its solution supplies techniques for understanding other self-adjusting trees and separates the cost of deleting minima from the harder decrease-key analysis.

importance.reason: Historically fundamental analysis of a canonical self-adjusting priority queue. The logarithmic delete-min target is now resolved, so this historical importance score does not place it ahead of open candidates.

progress.text: Fredman, Sedgewick, Sleator, and Tarjan introduce pairing heaps and the multipass variant. The original multipass analysis leaves a slowly growing factor above logarithmic cost.

Dorfman and coauthors improve the multipass delete-min upper bound to O(log n · log* n · 2^(log* n)) and explicitly retain the logarithmic target as open. The saved excerpt occurs on printed page 24:3.

Sinnamon and Tarjan announce the logarithmic amortized delete-min bound. Their multipass decrease-key bound is O(log log n · log log log n), while slim and smooth heaps attain O(log log n). These are different guarantees for different heap variants.
The revised paper states the multipass sequence bound as Theorem 7.18. The work appears in ACM Transactions on Algorithms 21(4), Article 37, and resolves the historical question retained here.

status_note: Resolved affirmatively by Sinnamon and Tarjan: 2023 preprint, revised 2025 and published in ACM TALG. Theorem 7.18 proves the requested logarithmic amortized delete-min bound. This does not assert a logarithmic worst-case bound or settle the companion path-balanced BST problem.
